strengths: The paper provides an in-depth explanation of the model architectures and training procedures for both M-LNN and P-LNN, as well as the noise structures used to augment synthetic data.
The introduction is well-written, and the motivation behind LPPLS is clearly laid out.
The overall idea to estimate LPPLS parameters with ML techniques also seems promising.
The real-world applications and comparison of different noise models are interesting.
This paper employs neural network tools to estimate the parameters of the LPPLS model, demonstrating superior accuracy and robustness compared to the standard Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) method.
The authors clearly delineate their methodology and experimental design.
The proposed technique plays a pivotal role in forecasting critical points, thereby holding significant relevance across natural, engineering, and economic systems.
I have not seen the LPPLS problem come up before in a scientific machine learning context, and it is a timely and worthwhile problem to study.
The paper is clearly written, and walks the reader very clearly through exactly what the authors did and how/why they did it.
A range of testing datasets was used, which span different domains and application areas relevant to practitioners.
weaknesses: The paper uses only three datasets, two of which focus on financial bubbles and the third rockslide example is insufficiently detailed, so claims about broad applicability to natural or engineering systems seem overstated.
The motivation for the penalty term is brief and limited to the specific financial domain, lacking a more general justification for priors/penalties in a general-purpose deep learning architecture.

The M-LNN model is a fully connected feedforward network without inductive biases for sequential or time-series data, and the paper does not explore more appropriate sequence models such as RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs, TCNs, or Transformers.
The P-LNN model accepts only a fixed input vector length of 252, undermining flexibility and requiring resampling of empirical datasets.
The paper provides no details on how the resampling to a fixed length of 252 observations is performed, including how much data is discarded or whether specific imputation methods are used.
Figure 2 shows a basic supervised training setup using vanilla gradient descent, which feels too simplistic for a major ML conference, and optimizer details are missing.
Figure 3’s text and legend linewidth could be larger to improve readability.
The results section lacks a thorough discussion of findings, providing only descriptions without analysis of what the results imply for model performance and limitations.
Claims that the NN models outperform the traditional LM method are not supported by in-depth comparisons such as statistical significance tests.
The paper may not yet be ready for a leading ML conference due to insufficient emphasis on architectural choices, methodological depth, and thorough evaluation.
The method integrates multi-layer neural networks with the LPPLS model without incorporating significantly novel designs, resulting in deficient innovation.

The experimental validation section fails to adequately substantiate the advantages of the proposed method and lacks a comprehensive explanation of why neural network strategies outperform conventional methodologies.
The LPPLS system is not widely applied, and the paper does not clearly explain why the problem is particularly important or difficult to fit with conventional methods.

Fitting only three parameters to time series data is a low-dimensional curve fitting task, raising questions about the necessity of neural networks over simpler methods like gradient descent or sequential parameter fitting.
The synthetic data used is very simple (LPPLS with autocorrelated white noise), and the dataset size is not justified as beneficial for a low-dimensional fitting problem.
Only one benchmark model is presented, and no ablation studies are included.

The P-LNN training procedure compares fitted parameters to ground truth rather than directly comparing LPPLS dynamics, making it a simple regression problem that could be solved by linear regression, which undermines its utility for real time series where parameters are unknown.
There is no clear train/test split, risking causal leakage, and the real data testing appears artificial with many choices in aligning series and parameter ranges, reducing robustness.
The code for the problem and application is not made available, hindering reproducibility.
